claim: Top enriched pathways in M2 macrophages include urea cycle and arginine and proline metabolism.
source: Top enriched pathways include urea cycle and arginine and proline metabolism, consistent with previous studies indicating upregulation of arginine metabolism in M2 macrophages (Van Dyken and Locksley, 2013), as well as amino acid utilization and metabolism and nucleotide metabolism (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data shown in Figure 1A and references a citation to Van Dyken and Locksley, 2013.

claim: M2 macrophages show enrichment in glycolysis, amino sugar metabolism, and glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism pathways.
source: Other top enriched pathways include glycolysis, amino sugar metabolism, and glycine, serine, and threonine metabolism, suggesting altered flux through glycolysis and glycolytic shunts (Figure 1A, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics profiling data presented in Figure 1A and Supplementary file 1.

claim: IL-4 treatment increases glucose uptake in BMDMs in a time-dependent manner.
source: We found that BMDMs increased glucose uptake in a time-dependent manner in response to IL-4 treatment.
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B measuring 3H-deoxy-D-glucose uptake.

claim: Akt inhibitor MK2206 reduces IL-4-induced glucose uptake in BMDMs.
source: Such increase was reduced by cotreatment with the Akt inhibitor MK2206 (Figure 1B), indicating control by Akt and consistent with a role for Akt in regulating glycolysis in many settings (Robey and Hay, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1B and a citation to Robey and Hay, 2009.

claim: Enhanced glucose consumption in M2 macrophages is associated with an Akt-dependent increase in both glycolysis and oxidative metabolism.
source: Moreover, enhanced glucose consumption in M2 macrophages was associated with an Akt-dependent increase in both glycolysis and oxidative metabolism, as indicated by extracellular flux assays (Figure 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by extracellular flux assay data presented in Figure 1C.

claim: The glycolysis inhibitor 2-DG reduces IL-4-mediated induction of some M2 genes.
source: Similar to the β-oxidation inhibitor etomoxir, the glycolysis inhibitor 2-DG reduced IL-4-mediated induction of some M2 genes (Figure 1D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Akt does not control β-oxidation in M2 macrophages.
source: In contrast, Akt does not control β-oxidation in M2 macrophages (Figure 1E).
evidence: The claim is supported by β-oxidation assay data presented in Figure 1E.

claim: Akt activity controls the induction of a subset of M2 genes including Arg1, Retnla, and Mgl2.
source: Importantly and as reported (Byles et al., 2013; Ruckerl et al., 2012), Akt activity controlled the induction of a subset of M2 genes. In the presence of the Akt inhibitor MK2206, induction of Arg1, Retnla, and Mgl2 was reduced ~40–80%, while Chi3l3, Cd36, and Fabp4 were not affected (or even super-inducible) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 2A and citations to Byles et al., 2013 and Ruckerl et al., 2012.

claim: Chi3l3, Cd36, and Fabp4 M2 gene induction is not affected by Akt inhibition.
source: In the presence of the Akt inhibitor MK2206, induction of Arg1, Retnla, and Mgl2 was reduced ~40–80%, while Chi3l3, Cd36, and Fabp4 were not affected (or even super-inducible) (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: IL-4-mediated increases in Stat6 activation are not affected by Akt inhibition.
source: Indeed, IL-4-mediated increases in Stat6 activation, as indicated by phosphorylation on Y641, was not affected in the presence of an Akt inhibitor (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2B.

claim: Stat6 activity measured by a Stat6-dependent luciferase reporter is not impaired by inhibition of Akt activity.
source: Stat6 activity as measured by a Stat6-dependent luciferase reporter was also not impaired by inhibition of Akt activity (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by luciferase assay data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: WT and Stat6 KO BMDMs can similarly activate Akt and mTORC1 in response to IL-4.
source: Conversely, WT and Stat6 KO BMDMs could similarly activate Akt, as indicated by phosphorylation on S473, as well as mTORC1, as indicated by phosphorylation of the mTORC1 target S6K, in response to IL-4 (Figure 2B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2B.

claim: The Jak-Stat and Akt-mTORC1 pathways are independent signaling branches downstream of the IL-4R.
source: These findings support the idea that the Jak-Stat and Akt-mTORC1 pathways are independent signaling branches downstream of the IL-4R, and suggest a basis by which all M2 genes are controlled by Stat6 while a subset receives additional inputs from the Akt-mTORC1 pathway.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the experimental data showing independent activation of Stat6 and Akt-mTORC1 pathways.

claim: IL-4 treatment enhances global acetylation of H3 and H4 histones in BMDMs.
source: Indeed, IL-4-treatment of BMDMs enhanced global acetylation of H3 and H4 histones, as indicated by western blot of whole cell lysates (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: IL-4-inducible increases in global H3 and H4 acetylation are reduced by Akt inhibitor cotreatment.
source: Importantly, IL-4-inducible increases in global H3 and H4 acetylation were reduced by cotreatment with an Akt inhibitor, indicating at least partial dependence on Akt (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: Tubulin acetylation is not modulated by IL-4 treatment.
source: In contrast, tubulin acetylation was not modulated by IL-4 treatment (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: IL-4 treatment increases H3 and H4 acetylation at promoters of M2 genes.
source: IL-4 treatment increased H3 and H4 acetylation at promoters of M2 genes (Figure 2D,E, Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), with the degree of inducible acetylation correlating fairly well with the degree of gene induction (Figure 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 2D, 2E, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Akt inhibitor reduces H3 and H4 acetylation at Akt-dependent M2 genes (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2) but not at Akt-independent M2 genes (Chi3l3, Cd36, Fabp4).
source: Interestingly, such increases in H3 and H4 acetylation were reduced by an Akt inhibitor at M2 genes induced in an Akt-dependent manner (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2), but not at M2 genes induced independently of Akt (Chi3l3, Cd36, Fabp4) (Figure 2D,E).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 2D and 2E.

claim: Pol II recruitment to M2 gene promoters parallels H3 and H4 acetylation and is controlled by Akt at Akt-dependent M2 genes.
source: Pol II recruitment to M2 gene promoters paralleled H3 and H4 acetylation, and was controlled by Akt at M2 genes induced in an Akt-dependent manner (Figure 2—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D.

claim: IL-4 treatment leads to a maximal increase in Ac-CoA levels of approximately 40-75%.
source: Using quantitative stable isotope dilution-LC-MS, we found that IL-4 treatment led to a maximal increase in Ac-CoA levels of ~40–75% (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS data in Figure 3A and 3C.

claim: IL-4 treatment stimulates the activating phosphorylation of Acly in an Akt-dependent manner.
source: Akt has been shown to phosphorylate and activate Acly (Berwick et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2014), and we found that in M2 macrophages, IL-4 treatment stimulated the activating phosphorylation of Acly in an Akt-dependent manner (Figure 3B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, and citations to Berwick et al., 2002 and Lee et al., 2014.

claim: Cotreatment with Akt or Acly inhibitors blocks IL-4-mediated increases in Ac-CoA levels.
source: Importantly, cotreatment with Akt or Acly inhibitors blocked the IL-4-mediated increases in Ac-CoA levels (Figure 3C), indicating Akt- and Acly-mediated control of Ac-CoA production in M2 macrophages.
evidence: The claim is supported by LC-MS data in Figure 3C.

claim: Citrate accumulates in the presence of Akt or Acly inhibitors.
source: Conversely, citrate, the substrate for the Acly reaction, accumulated in the presence of the inhibitors (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The claim is supported by metabolomics data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: IL-4 treatment enhances 13C (M+2) Ac-CoA labeling from glucose, palmitate, and glutamine tracers.
source: IL-4 treatment enhanced 13C (M+2) Ac-CoA labeling regardless of the tracer, indicating that all three metabolic fuels contributed to the elevated Ac-CoA pool.
evidence: The claim is supported by carbon tracing LC-MS data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Palmitate is the major carbon source for Ac-CoA in M2 macrophages.
source: The highest labeling was observed in BMDMs fed palmitate. While LC-MS does not specifically measure the nuclear-cytosolic pool of Ac-CoA, these data suggests that palmitate may be the major carbon source for histone acetylation in M2 macrophages (Figure 3D).
evidence: The claim is inferred from carbon tracing data in Figure 3D showing highest labeling with palmitate.

claim: The Acly inhibitor SB-204990 reduces IL-4-mediated induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2) but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Chi3l3, Fabp4, Cd36).
source: Indeed, the Acly inhibitor SB-204990 reduced IL-4-mediated induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes (Arg1, Retnla, Mgl2) but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Chi3l3, Fabp4, Cd36) (Figure 4A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4A.

claim: SB-204990 treatment attenuates IL-4-mediated increases in H3 and H4 acetylation at promoters of Akt-dependent M2 genes but not Akt-independent M2 genes.
source: Moreover, SB-204990 treatment attenuated IL-4-mediated increases in H3 and H4 acetylation at promoters of Akt-dependent M2 genes, but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SB-204990 treatment diminishes Pol II recruitment at Akt-dependent M2 genes.
source: Likewise, SB-204990 treatment diminished Pol II recruitment at Akt-dependent M2 genes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by ChIP data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The p300 inhibitor C646 reduces induction of Akt-dependent but not Akt-independent M2 genes.
source: Interestingly, the p300 inhibitor C646 reduced induction of Akt-dependent but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Figure 4C).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4C.

claim: p300 may link the Akt/Acly-dependent rise in Ac-CoA levels to increased histone acetylation and gene induction at some Akt-dependent M2 genes.
source: Therefore, p300 may link the Akt/Acly-dependent rise in Ac-CoA levels to increased histone acetylation and gene induction at some Akt-dependent M2 genes, while distinct HATs at Akt-independent genes are insensitive to such modulation of Ac-CoA levels.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the p300 inhibitor data and knowledge about p300's sensitivity to Ac-CoA levels.

claim: Arginase activity is regulated by Acly and Akt.
source: Consistent with effects on induction of Arg1, arginase activity was regulated by Acly and Akt (Figure 4D).
evidence: The claim is supported by arginase activity assay data in Figure 4D.

claim: Akt and Acly inhibitors reduce induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes in peritoneal-elicited macrophages.
source: Additionally, Akt and Acly inhibitors reduced induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes in peritoneal-elicited macrophages, indicating that control of M2 activation by the Akt-Acly axis may be applicable to multiple macrophage populations (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes is deficient in BMDMs lacking Raptor.
source: Indeed, we found that induction of Akt-dependent M2 genes was deficient in BMDMs lacking Raptor, a defining subunit of the mTORC1 complex (Dibble and Manning, 2013). In contrast, induction of Akt-independent M2 genes was not reduced (Figure 5A).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 5A and a citation to Dibble and Manning, 2013.

claim: Raptor-deficient BMDMs express lower levels of Acly protein.
source: mTORC1 is known to stimulate Acly expression (Porstmann et al., 2008; Düvel et al., 2010), and we found that Raptor-deficient BMDMs expressed lower levels of Acly protein (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 5B and citations to Porstmann et al., 2008 and Düvel et al., 2010.

claim: BMDMs with constitutive mTORC1 activity from Tsc1 deletion display elevated Acly levels that are reduced by rapamycin treatment.
source: Conversely, BMDMs with constitutive mTORC1 activity resulting from deletion of Tsc1 (Byles et al., 2013), a negative regulator of mTORC1 (Dibble and Manning, 2013), displayed elevated Acly levels that were reduced by treatment with the mTORC1 inhibitor rapamycin (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1 and citations to Byles et al., 2013 and Dibble and Manning, 2013.

claim: IL-4-inducible Acly phosphorylation is reduced in Raptor-deficient BMDMs.
source: Additionally, we noted that IL-4-inducible Acly phosphorylation was reduced in Raptor-deficient BMDMs (Figure 5B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 5B.

claim: The Akt-mTORC1 axis controls Acly activating phosphorylation and protein levels.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that the Akt-mTORC1 axis controls Acly activating phosphorylation and protein levels, likely contributing to its control of M2 activation.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the combined data on Akt and mTORC1 regulation of Acly.

claim: mTORC1 activity is greatly reduced in amino acid deficient media and intermediate in media containing low levels of amino acids.
source: As expected, mTORC1 activity, as assessed by phosphorylation of its downstream target S6K, was greatly reduced in amino acid deficient media and intermediate in media containing low levels of amino acids (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6B.

claim: Increasing amino acid levels augments Akt activation.
source: In line with (Tato et al., 2011; Novellasdemunt et al., 2013), increasing amino acid levels also augmented Akt activation, as indicated by enhanced phosphorylation on two critical residues, T308 and S473 (Figure 6B).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6B and citations to Tato et al., 2011 and Novellasdemunt et al., 2013.

claim: Titrating amino acids has no effect on Stat6 phosphorylation and activation.
source: Titrating amino acids had no effect on Stat6 phosphorylation and activation (Figure 6B), validating the use of this experimental model to modulate the Akt-mTORC1 axis independent of canonical Stat6 signaling.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6B.

claim: Amino acid levels dose dependently increase Acly phosphorylation and protein levels.
source: Consistent with effects on mTORC1 and Akt activity, amino acid levels dose dependently increased Acly phosphorylation and protein levels (Figure 6B) as well as Ac-CoA production (Figure 6C).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6B and LC-MS data in Figure 6C.

claim: Amino acids potentiate induction of Akt-dependent but not Akt-independent M2 genes.
source: Importantly, amino acids potentiated induction of Akt-dependent but not Akt-independent M2 genes (Figure 6D).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6D.

claim: The effect of amino acids on M2 gene induction is at least partially Raptor-dependent.
source: This effect of amino acids was at least partially Raptor-dependent, indicating a critical role for mTORC1 in this process (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Culture in leucine-deficient media attenuates IL-4-inducible mTORC1 and Akt activity and Acly phosphorylation, but not Stat6 phosphorylation.
source: Culture in leucine-deficient media attenuated IL-4-inducible mTORC1 and Akt activity and Acly phosphorylation, but not Stat6 phosphorylation (Figure 6E).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6E.

claim: Leucine deficiency selectively reduces expression of Akt-dependent M2 genes.
source: Importantly, leucine deficiency selectively reduced expression of Akt-dependent M2 genes (Figure 6F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6F.

claim: Akt activation is increased in the fed state compared to the fasted state in the ATM-containing stromal vascular fraction of white adipose tissue.
source: Specifically, we found that Akt activation was increased in the fed state compared to the fasted state in the ATM-containing stromal vascular (SVF) fraction of the white adipose tissue (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A.

claim: Global H3 acetylation and M2 gene expression are elevated in the fed state in adipose tissue macrophages.
source: Although we were unable to reliably detect pAcly or Acly in the SVF for technical reasons, global H3 acetylation (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B) and M2 gene expression (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C) followed a similar pattern and were elevated in the fed state.
evidence: The claim is supported by western blot data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2A-B and qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: IL-13 expression is increased in the fed state.
source: Expression of all M2 genes was elevated in the fed state (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C), consistent with an important role for IL-13, a critical regulator of ATM M2 polarization (Odegaard and Chawla, 2011) that is increased in the fed state (Figure 6—figure supplement 2D), in feeding-induced ATM polarization, although postprandial elevations in nutrients like amino acids and glucose may also contribute.
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 6—figure supplement 2D and a citation to Odegaard and Chawla, 2011.

claim: 758 genes were induced >2.0 fold by IL-4 in BMDMs.
source: In the RNA seq analysis, 758 genes were induced >2.0 fold by IL-4, of which 91were downregulated >30% by both Akt and Acly inhibitors (including Arg1, Retnla, and Mgl2), confirming critical roles for Akt and Acly in control of M2 activation as well as substantial overlap in the activities of the two proteins (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: 91 IL-4-inducible genes were downregulated >30% by both Akt and Acly inhibitors.
source: In the RNA seq analysis, 758 genes were induced >2.0 fold by IL-4, of which 91were downregulated >30% by both Akt and Acly inhibitors (including Arg1, Retnla, and Mgl2), confirming critical roles for Akt and Acly in control of M2 activation as well as substantial overlap in the activities of the two proteins (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data presented in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Most genes sensitive to Acly inhibitor are sensitive to Akt inhibitor (91/118).
source: In contrast, most genes sensitive to Acly inhibitor were sensitive to Akt inhibitor (91/118). This indicates that in the context of M2 activation, Acly is a major target of Akt and is critically controlled by Akt activity, likely in regulation of Ac-CoA production and histone acetylation at M2 genes (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: The claim is supported by RNA-seq data analysis presented in Figure 7A and 7B.

claim: Cell cycle and DNA replication pathways are preferentially enriched among the 91 Akt- and Acly-coregulated genes.
source: Gene enrichment analysis of the 91 Akt- and Acly-coregulated genes identified preferential enrichment of several pathways, including cell cycle and DNA replication (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: The claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis data in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: Chemokines are enriched in Akt- and Acly-coregulated genes, including Ccl2, Ccl7, Ccl17, and Ccl24.
source: Interestingly, chemokines were also enriched in Akt- and Acly-coregulated genes (Figure 7C–D), including Ccl2, Ccl7, Ccl17, and Ccl24.
evidence: The claim is supported by gene enrichment analysis data in Figure 7C and 7D.

claim: Akt- and Acly-dependent induction of CCL17 and CCL24 was confirmed by qRT-PCR and ELISA.
source: Akt- and Acly-dependent induction of CCL17 and CCL24 was confirmed by qRT-PCR and ELISA (Figure 7E–F).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 7E and ELISA data in Figure 7F.

claim: Ear2, Ear11, and Ear12 genes are coregulated by the Akt-Acly pathway.
source: Finally, genes in the eosinophil associated ribonucleases (Ear) family were found to be regulated by Akt and Acly. While barely missing the stringent cutoffs that we set for the RNA-seq analysis, qPCR analysis confirmed coregulation of Ear2, Ear11, and Ear12 genes by the Akt-Acly pathway (Figure 7E).
evidence: The claim is supported by qPCR data in Figure 7E.

claim: IL-4 signaling co-opts the Akt-mTORC1 pathway to regulate Acly, leading to increased histone acetylation and M2 gene induction.
source: Here we show that IL-4 signaling co-opts the Akt-mTORC1 pathway to regulate Acly, a key enzyme in Ac-CoA synthesis, leading to increased histone acetylation and M2 gene induction.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the combined experimental data throughout the manuscript.

claim: Only a subset of M2 genes is controlled by the Akt-mTORC1-Acly pathway, including those regulating cellular proliferation and chemokine production.
source: Only a subset of M2 genes is controlled in this way, including those regulating cellular proliferation and chemokine production.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the RNA-seq and gene enrichment analysis data.

claim: Metabolic signals impinge on the Akt-mTORC1 axis for control of M2 activation.
source: Moreover, metabolic signals impinge on the Akt-mTORC1 axis for such control of M2 activation.
evidence: This is a summary claim supported by the amino acid titration and leucine deficiency experiments.

claim: Akt-mTORC1 signaling calibrates metabolic state to energetically demanding aspects of M2 activation.
source: We propose that Akt-mTORC1 signaling calibrates metabolic state to energetically demanding aspects of M2 activation, which may define a new role for metabolism in supporting macrophage activation.
evidence: This is a proposed model based on the combined experimental findings.

claim: M1 macrophages upregulate glucose and glutamine utilization.
source: For example, M1 macrophages upregulate glucose and glutamine utilization (Tannahill et al., 2013; Cramer et al., 2003), while M2 macrophages augment β-oxidation and glutamine consumption (Vats et al., 2006; Jha et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Tannahill et al., 2013 and Cramer et al., 2003.

claim: M2 macrophages augment β-oxidation and glutamine consumption.
source: For example, M1 macrophages upregulate glucose and glutamine utilization (Tannahill et al., 2013; Cramer et al., 2003), while M2 macrophages augment β-oxidation and glutamine consumption (Vats et al., 2006; Jha et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Vats et al., 2006 and Jha et al., 2015.

claim: Increased glycolytic flux in M1 macrophages is coupled to de novo lipogenesis, which enables ER and Golgi expansion and production of high levels of inflammatory cytokines.
source: Increased glycolytic flux in M1 macrophages is coupled to de novo lipogenesis, which enables ER and Golgi expansion and production of high levels of inflammatory cytokines (Everts et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Everts et al., 2014.

claim: Enhanced glycolysis in M1 macrophages leads to accumulation of succinate, resulting in stabilization of HIF-1α and transcriptional induction of Il1b.
source: Another consequence of enhanced glycolysis is accumulation of the TCA cycle metabolite succinate, leading to stabilization of the transcription factor HIF-1α and transcriptional induction of Il1b and other target genes in the M1 macrophage (Tannahill et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Tannahill et al., 2013.

claim: Glutamine metabolism fuels production of UDP-GlcNAC, an important modification of multiple M2 markers.
source: How oxidative metabolism boosts M2 activation is not clear, but glutamine metabolism fuels production of UDP-GlcNAC, an important modification of multiple M2 markers (Jha et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Jha et al., 2015.

claim: Akt mediates enhanced glycolysis to support lipid synthesis and inflammatory cytokine secretion in M1 macrophages.
source: For example, Akt mediates enhanced glycolysis to support lipid synthesis and inflammatory cytokine secretion in M1 macrophages (Everts et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Everts et al., 2014.

claim: Akt stimulates glucose-fueled lipid synthesis in growing and proliferating cells, where lipids are used to build cellular membranes.
source: Akt similarly stimulates glucose-fueled lipid synthesis in growing and proliferating cells, where lipids are used to build cellular membranes (Robey and Hay, 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Robey and Hay, 2009.

claim: In cancer cells and differentiating adipocytes, metabolic state is linked to gene expression via effects on histone acetylation.
source: A seminal study from Wellen and colleagues indicated that in cancer cells and differentiating adipocytes, metabolic state is linked to gene expression via effects on histone acetylation (Wellen et al., 2009), thus we hypothesized that Akt may control histone acetylation to regulate M2 gene expression.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wellen et al., 2009.

claim: Acly cleaves cytosolic citrate to produce a nuclear-cytoplasmic pool of Ac-CoA.
source: A key regulator of Ac-CoA production is the enzyme Acly, which cleaves cytosolic citrate to produce a nuclear-cytoplasmic pool of Ac-CoA (Wellen et al., 2009).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Wellen et al., 2009 and established biochemical knowledge.

claim: The activity of some HATs, including p300, is regulated by Ac-CoA levels and metabolic status.
source: The activity of some HATs, including p300, is regulated by Ac-CoA levels and metabolic status (Mariño et al., 2014; Pietrocola et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mariño et al., 2014 and Pietrocola et al., 2015.

claim: mTORC1 activity in macrophages is controlled by amino acid levels, ADP/ATP levels, and other metabolic inputs.
source: The Akt-mTORC1 pathway is a major metabolic sensor, and mTORC1 activity in particular is controlled by amino acid levels, ADP/ATP levels, and other metabolic inputs (Dibble and Manning, 2013; Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dibble and Manning, 2013 and Laplante and Sabatini, 2012.

claim: Amino acids directly and potently regulate mTORC1 activity independent of the TSC complex.
source: Amino acids directly and potently regulate mTORC1 activity independent of the TSC complex (Dibble and Manning, 2013; Laplante and Sabatini, 2012) and can also activate Akt in some contexts (Tato et al., 2011; Novellasdemunt et al., 2013), hence we varied amino acid concentrations as a way to modulate Akt-mTORC1 activity.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Dibble and Manning, 2013 and Laplante and Sabatini, 2012.

claim: Leucine is particularly critical in regulation of mTORC1 activity.
source: We also examined M2 activation using the complementary model of leucine deprivation, since leucine is particularly critical in regulation of mTORC1 activity (Hara et al., 1998).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hara et al., 1998.

claim: ATM M2 polarization is thought to critically maintain insulin sensitivity in white adipose tissue.
source: ATM M2 polarization is thought to critically maintain insulin sensitivity in white adipose tissue, so such feeding-induced increases in M2 activation may coordinate responses to nutrient influx to mediate metabolic homeostasis in the postprandial state (Odegaard and Chawla, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Odegaard and Chawla, 2011.

claim: p300 has a high Km for Ac-CoA and is responsive to changes in Ac-CoA levels.
source: Its high Km (Mariño et al., 2014; Pietrocola et al., 2015) may allow p300 to link metabolic status and Akt/mTORC1 activity, in the form of Ac-CoA levels, to histone acetylation and transcriptional induction at some M2 genes (Figure 7—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Mariño et al., 2014 and Pietrocola et al., 2015.

claim: Aberrantly increased mTORC1 activity in Tsc1-deficient BMDMs attenuates M2 activation.
source: In seeming contrast to these data indicating that mTORC1 supports M2 activation, we and others have shown that aberrantly increased mTORC1 activity in Tsc1-deficient BMDMs attenuates M2 activation (Byles et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Byles et al., 2013 and Zhu et al., 2014.

claim: In obesity, chronic nutrient excess leads to an aberrant increase in mTORC1 activity that contributes directly to insulin resistance and metabolic dysregulation.
source: Downstream of the insulin receptor, such context-dependent roles of mTORC1 are well-established. In lean/healthy animals, mTORC1 critically mediates insulin signaling in metabolic tissues (to coordinate postprandial nutrient storage), but in obesity, chronic nutrient excess leads to an aberrant increase in mTORC1 activity that contributes directly to insulin resistance and metabolic dysregulation (Laplante and Sabatini, 2012).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Laplante and Sabatini, 2012.

claim: Ac-CoA can be synthesized independently of the Akt-mTORC1-Acly axis by AceCS1 or nuclear pyruvate dehydrogenase.
source: Alternatively, Ac-CoA can be synthesized independently of the Akt-mTORC1-Acly axis by AceCS1 (Hallows et al., 2006) or nuclear pyruvate dehydrogenase (Sutendra et al., 2014) to mediate histone acetylation.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Hallows et al., 2006 and Sutendra et al., 2014.

claim: AceCS1 activity is controlled by SIRT1, providing a means for Ac-CoA production and histone acetylation in conditions of low energy or nutrients.
source: AceCS1 activity is controlled by SIRT1, thus providing a means for Ac-CoA production and histone acetylation in conditions of low energy or nutrients (Hallows et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Hallows et al., 2006.

claim: Ear2 and Ear11 are thought to have chemoattractant activity for dendritic cells and macrophages.
source: Ear genes are of interest because Ear2 and Ear11 are thought to have chemoattractant activity for dendritic cells and macrophages and are known to be highly induced in settings of Type 2 inflammation (Cormier et al., 2002; Yamada et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Cormier et al., 2002 and Yamada et al., 2015.

claim: M2 macrophages play a key role in metabolic homeostasis, parasite infection, allergic diseases, and wound healing and tissue repair.
source: As M2 macrophages play a key role in metabolic homeostasis, parasite infection, allergic diseases, and wound healing and tissue repair (Van Dyken and Locksley, 2013; Odegaard and Chawla, 2011), these findings are relevant for metabolic control of macrophage function in diverse contexts.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Van Dyken and Locksley, 2013 and Odegaard and Chawla, 2011.

claim: The Akt-mTORC1 pathway has a well-established role in promoting anabolic metabolism in growing/proliferating cells, tumor cells, and metabolic tissues.
source: The Akt-mTORC1 pathway has a well-established role in promoting anabolic metabolism in growing/proliferating cells, tumor cells, and metabolic tissues.
evidence: This is a statement of established scientific knowledge.

claim: In the context of cellular proliferation, Akt-mTORC1 activity couples growth factor signaling and nutrient availability to the synthesis of proteins, lipids, and nucleotides.
source: In the context of cellular proliferation, for example, Akt-mTORC1 activity couples growth factor signaling and nutrient availability to the synthesis of proteins, lipids, and nucleotides (Dibble and Manning, 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dibble and Manning, 2013.

claim: A critical role for Akt-mTORC1 signaling in activated CD8 T cells is to support their migration to sites of inflammation.
source: Interestingly, previous studies have shown that a critical role for Akt-mTORC1 signaling in activated CD8 T cells is to support their migration to sites of inflammation (Finlay and Cantrell, 2011).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Finlay and Cantrell, 2011.
